body:
London music history is usually attached to vanished clubs, famous studios and blue plaques. Music videos preserve something different: an ordinary pavement, a railway bridge, a corner shop or a café at one particular moment.

I returned to four locations with frames from the original videos. The exercise is less about recreating the performers’ poses than testing what the camera recorded. Buildings survive, businesses disappear, signs change and a street that looked anonymous becomes recognisable once the right image is placed beside it.

The historic images in this article are frames from the official videos, used to identify and discuss the locations. The contemporary photographs are mine.

## Rick Astley beneath the railway

*Never Gonna Give You Up* was filmed in 1987 at several west London locations. The exterior most often mistaken for somewhere in Harrow is actually on Freston Road, close to Latimer Road station, beneath the Hammersmith and City line viaduct.

The confusion has an explanation. Other scenes were filmed inside the nearby Harrow Club, whose name led many later descriptions in the wrong geographical direction. The club is in North Kensington, not Harrow.

The bridge is still easy to recognise. Brick arches, the curve of the road and the compressed space beneath the tracks do most of the work. What seemed like an anonymous background became one of the most repeatedly watched pieces of London through the later phenomenon of Rickrolling.

There is no attraction to enter. It remains a working street under a railway. The interesting part is precisely that mismatch between the global reach of the image and the ordinariness of the place.

## Richard Ashcroft walks through Hoxton

The 1997 video for *Bitter Sweet Symphony* follows Richard Ashcroft north along the eastern side of Hoxton Street. The walk begins around the junction with Falkirk Street and is presented as one relentless forward movement, with Ashcroft refusing to alter his path for other pedestrians.

Hoxton has changed substantially since the 1990s, but this section has not become unrecognisable. Shop names and uses have changed, while the pavement line, estate buildings and proportions of the street still hold the shot together. The former Golden Fried Chicken at the start of the sequence is now another chicken shop, an unusually modest form of continuity.

Trying to reproduce Ashcroft’s collisions would be idiotic. Standing back and comparing the shopfront rhythm is more revealing. The video turned a local shopping street into an image of 1990s British confidence and abrasion without disguising where it was filmed.

A year later, the video for Fat Les’s *Vindaloo* parodied the same walk on the same street. Hoxton therefore contains both the original piece of pop mythology and its almost immediate joke.

## Dexys on Brook Drive

*Come On Eileen* was filmed in 1982 around Brook Drive in Kennington, between Elephant and Castle and the Imperial War Museum. Several corners appear, but the best-known storefront stood at 151 Brook Drive, at the junction with Hayles Street.

In the video it was Vi’s Stores. The band perform and move through streets of late Victorian terraces, parked cars, small shops and vacant land. The setting feels unstaged because much of it was simply the neighbourhood as it stood.

The shop later became Brook Drive Minimarket and has since closed. Yet this is the pair of images in which the surrounding brickwork makes the comparison particularly effective. The business identity has gone, while the corner remains legible more than four decades later.

This is also why music videos can become accidental urban records. Nobody watching in 1982 needed the film to explain what a south London corner shop looked like. That ordinary information is now one of its most interesting qualities.

## a-ha at the café on Wandsworth Road

The live-action café scenes in a-ha’s 1985 video for *Take On Me* were filmed at Kim’s Café, on the corner of Wandsworth Road and Pensbury Place. The premises later traded as the Savoy Café and are now occupied by a Turkish restaurant.

Most of the video’s reputation rests on the transition between live action and pencil animation. Around 3,000 frames were rotoscoped, turning the café customer, played by Bunty Bailey, and Morten Harket’s comic-book character into one continuous story.

The London exterior is easy to overlook because the fantasy takes over so quickly. Returning to the corner brings the video back to its practical starting point: a small café, a cup of coffee and someone reading alone at a table.

Unlike the other three locations, this is an operating business rather than just a public street. The façade can be compared from the pavement. Going inside should mean behaving like a customer, not treating the restaurant as a film set.

## Four famous images, no formal trail

These locations do not form a sensible single walk. They stretch from North Kensington to Hoxton, Kennington and Wandsworth Road. Visiting them separately, when another journey takes you nearby, is more honest than manufacturing a cross-London itinerary.

Save the relevant official video before going and pause on the frame you want to match. Small alignments matter more than dramatic poses: the edge of an arch, the angle of a shopfront, a line of windows or the width of the pavement.

The reward is not nostalgia alone. It is seeing how popular culture fixes ordinary London in memory, while the real city continues changing around the frame.
dek: Rick Astley under a railway viaduct, Richard Ashcroft crossing Hoxton, Dexys on a Kennington corner and a-ha inside a south London café. Four famous videos left precise traces in ordinary streets.
